item.text: The file has 90 measurements: three specimens each for aluminum, steel, and titanium, with 10 points per specimen. The strain range is consistently 0.0002–0.0020, so I’ll fit each material across that shared range and show individual specimen measurements alongside the material-level fits.

item.aggregated_output:
# Tensile test analysis

Elastic modulus was estimated by an ordinary least-squares linear fit of stress versus strain, pooling the 30 measurements (three specimens × 10 points) for each material. The fitted slope is the modulus; the intercept was allowed to vary. Fits cover the measured strain range, 0.0002–0.0020 mm/mm.

| Material | Elastic modulus (GPa) | Fit intercept (MPa) | R² |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Aluminum | 69.38 | -0.31 | 0.99834 |
| Steel | 199.06 | 0.62 | 0.99844 |
| Titanium | 116.56 | -0.77 | 0.99788 |

![Stress–strain measurements and pooled linear fits](stress_strain_fits.svg)

The measurements are strongly linear over the sampled range (R² ≥ 0.9979). Steel has the largest estimated modulus, followed by titanium and aluminum. These are pooled, range-specific estimates; the CSV does not identify an elastic-region cutoff or provide points near zero strain, so the fit range is taken as the elastic region and the small fitted intercepts should not be interpreted as a measured preload.

item.text:
Analyzed the 30 measurements per material with pooled linear fits over the measured strain range. The estimated moduli are **69.38 GPa** for aluminum, **199.06 GPa** for steel, and **116.56 GPa** for titanium.

The write-up and figure are saved in [results.md](/private/tmp/tmpyy98c21w/pete/projects/elastic-modulus/results.md) and [stress_strain_fits.svg](/private/tmp/tmpyy98c21w/pete/projects/elastic-modulus/stress_strain_fits.svg). I also saved the reproducible analysis script as [analyze_measurements.py](/private/tmp/tmpyy98c21w/pete/projects/elastic-modulus/analyze_measurements.py).
